title: Ashtpadi 9, salok: the true names
hook: the salok turns to what the true devotee is like

segments.voice: Yesterday, gareebee: a child in her father's shoes, and a portrait to grow into. Your line was grow into it. Today, ashtpadi nine.

Every age has its religious job titles. Reverend. Doctor of divinity. Elder. In Guru Arjan's Punjab, around 1600, people heard plenty too: pandit, the learned one; vaishnav, the devotee of Vishnu; and aparas, the untouched one, a holy man who kept himself ritually apart, never touching anything that might make him impure. Ashtpadi nine takes these honored names one by one. It doesn't mock them. It does something more interesting: it asks what each name would look like if it were true all the way through.
screen: `EVERY AGE HAS ITS TITLES.` → `PANDIT, VAISHNAV, APARAS.` → `WHAT IF EACH WERE TRUE?`

segments.voice: The salok begins with the last of those names. Whoever keeps the Name enshrined in the heart, sees God in everyone, and bows to the Master moment by moment: Nanak, that one is the true aparas, and saves all. Notice the swap. The aparas of the day kept apart from other people to stay pure. Guru Arjan's aparas sees God in everyone, the opposite of keeping apart. The purity is still there, but it's moved: not what your hands avoid, but what your heart holds. The first stanza fills it in: the true aparas is one whose tongue never touches a lie, whose eyes don't look with lust at another's spouse, who loves the company of the holy. The untouched one is untouched by falsehood. That's the pattern of the whole ashtpadi. Each stanza takes a respected title and pours new content into it, a life to match the name. It says nothing against the people who held those titles sincerely. It just won't let the name do the work by itself. This fits the Sikh path closely. Sikhism has no priestly caste. A granthi who reads in the gurdwara is a respected servant of the community, not a holy class apart, and any Sikh, woman or man, may read the Guru Granth Sahib. So ashtpadi nine keeps asking not what are you called, but what are you like.
screen: `APARAS: THE UNTOUCHED ONE.` · `NOT APART: SEEING GOD IN ALL.` · `UNTOUCHED BY FALSEHOOD.` · `A LIFE TO MATCH THE NAME.` · then, large: `TRUE, NOT TITLED.`

segments.voice: Picture someone with an impressive title, a doctor, a judge, a religious leader, and then someone with no title at all who is completely trustworthy, and ask which one you'd call at two in the morning. Let that answer settle, then turn the question, gently, toward yourself: not what you're called, but what you're like when no one's watching.
Aparas, the untouched one. Not the one who keeps apart, but the one who sees God in all.
Your line: true, not titled. A name is only as true as the life under it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhism has no priestly caste: any Sikh may read the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs read ashtpadi nine of Sukhmani Sahib as a call to live up to a name rather than rest on it.

chat.says: Holy men once kept 'untouched' to stay pure. What did Guru Arjan make of that?
options: He moved the purity: the true aparas sees God in everyone and is untouched by falsehood.
He praised it, and asked Sikhs to keep apart from other people to stay pure.
He mocked those holy men and told everyone to drop every religious title.
chat.meaning: The salok's true aparas keeps the Name in the heart and sees God in all: purity moves from the hands to the heart.
